coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage would mean: of the AWS services that exist, how many have at least one AWS Config managed rule evaluating them. This page gives you NOTHING for that. It never names a service. The only route to a service is guessing from the rule-name prefix, and that is inference, not a stated claim — and the prefixes are unreliable: alb-* is Elastic Load Balancing v2 not a service called "alb"; acmpca-certificate-authority-tagged and acm-pca-root-ca-disabled use two different spellings for AWS Private CA; virtualmachine-* rules belong to AWS Backup, not to any "virtualmachine" service; vpc-sg-* rules evaluate Amazon EC2 security groups. Do not derive a service list here.

REGION coverage would mean: for each managed rule, in which AWS Regions is it available — AWS publishes exactly that elsewhere, as a rule-by-Region availability table. This page gives you NOTHING. The word "Region" does not appear on it, not once. Any Region claim built from this page is fabricated.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage would mean: which AWS Config resource types (AWS::EC2::Instance, AWS::S3::Bucket, …) are evaluated by at least one managed rule. This page gives you NOTHING. Resource type is stated on each individual rule's page, under its trigger/scope, and is absent from this index.

What the page does give you is the complete membership of AWS Config's own rule catalogue: 822 rule identifiers. That is a self-catalogue, so it answers "what rules exist", never "how much of the AWS surface Config reaches". All three real coverage dimensions require fetching the 822 child pages; this page is only the index that tells you which 822 to fetch.

features.reasoning: The page documents exactly one capability, and the values are managed rule names — the identifier you pass as the rule's source identifier / configRuleName, e.g. access-keys-rotated, vpc-default-security-group-closed. Count method: the file is 834 lines; lines 9–830 are the list; `grep -c '^+ \['` gives 822 bullets, lines 9–830 contain 822 bullets and 0 non-bullet lines, and `sort -u` on the extracted names also gives 822, so there are no duplicates. Distinct link targets are 824 = 822 rule pages + evaluate-config.md (the Considerations link) + the agent-toolkit URL in See also, which cross-checks the 822. The axis is a CATALOGUE, not external: these rules exist only because AWS Config publishes them, so AWS Config holds 822/822 = 100% of them by definition. A percentage on this axis measures nothing and must never be rendered as a coverage ratio. The correct use of this page is as an enumeration of the catalogue — a seed list and a join key into the 822 per-rule pages, where the real external axes (resource type, Region, trigger type) actually live.
features.statuses: 822 stated as supported, 0 stated as not supported. The lead sentence is the only status statement on the page: "AWS Config currently supports the following managed rules." Everything listed is therefore supported by construction. I searched the full page text for every exclusion signal AWS normally uses — "deprecated", "retired", "legacy", "no longer", "not supported", "unsupported", "except" — and for the word "Region": zero matches. There is no Yes/No column (the page contains no table pipes at all), no footnote marker, and no negative prose. So the not-covered side of this axis is empty on this page, and that emptiness is a fact about the page, not an inference.

pageTitle: List of AWS Config Managed Rules
shouldNotExtract: - The "**Topics**" label itself, and the fact that the list is formatted as a Topics block — the label is chrome, though here the items under it are the content (see trap). - The lead-in cross reference "see [Considerations](evaluate-config.md#evaluate-config-considerations)" — a pointer to prerequisites, not a value. - The whole "## See also" section, including the appended boilerplate bullet "**Skills for AI coding assistants (optional).** AWS publishes reusable skills for AWS Config… `aws agent-toolkit search-skills --search-query config`… Agent Toolkit for AWS". That bullet is on every AWS page now, mentions a CLI command and a docs link, and is neither a rule nor a covered thing. It also contributes 2 of the 824 distinct link targets, so it must be excluded before any count is cross-checked against link counts. - The `` anchor. - The `.md` link targets as values — the value is the rule name in the link text, not the filename.
trap:
Two traps, pulling in opposite directions.

First and worst: the general rule "never extract Topics blocks" deletes this entire page. The 822 rule names sit inside a **Topics** block and nowhere else. A parser that strips Topics blocks as navigation yields zero values here and reports the page as having no coverage content. The rule has to be "a Topics block is navigation unless it is the page's only enumeration and the lead sentence declares it as the supported set" — which is exactly this page: "AWS Config currently supports the following managed rules."

Second: extracting the 822 and presenting them as coverage. 822 of 822 supported is 100% by construction, because the set is AWS Config's own catalogue. Reporting "AWS Config: 100% coverage" from this page is a true sentence that means nothing. Worse is the next step a careless parser takes — bucketing the rule names by their leading token (ec2 57, rds 38, sagemaker 35, s3 29, iam 22, …) and publishing that as service coverage or as per-service rule counts. The page states no service for any rule, and the prefixes are not service names.

Minor trap: counting the 824 distinct link targets instead of the 822 bullets, which silently adds the Considerations link and the Agent Toolkit link.
whatThePageStates: This is the index page for AWS Config managed rules. It carries one sentence of prose — "AWS Config currently supports the following managed rules. Before using these rules, see Considerations" — followed by a single **Topics** block of 822 links, one per managed rule, in alphabetical order by rule name (access-keys-rotated … workspaces-workspace-tagged), each pointing at that rule's own page. There is no table, no Yes/No column, no Region column, no footnote, and no prose anywhere on the page other than that one sentence plus a "See also" bullet. The page enumerates AWS Config's own rule catalogue and nothing else: it never names an AWS service, a Region, or a resource type.
